subject: ela
text: Before the word work, here’s a little secret. Long words are often built from smaller pieces, the way a castle is built from stones. Today you’ll find two of those pieces and figure out what each one means, before the page tells you. After that come some joining words and some vowel pairs. Take it one step at a time.

subject: ela
text: Before you open the book: Chapter 1 has a feast, a prank, and a boy in a cold tower. As you read, keep asking yourself who gives the orders, and who has to obey. And listen to how Jemmy talks. He grew up on the city streets, and the author wants you to hear it.

subject: ela
text: Now it’s your turn to have an opinion. A good claim names a character, says what you think of them, and hints at why. You can pick any character, as long as the book gives you a reason. Think back over the feast and the lessons. Then write your claim in one strong sentence.

subject: ela
text: Jemmy talks like the streets he grew up on. Words like ain’t and me rags aren’t mistakes. The author wrote them on purpose so you can hear Jemmy in your head. Tap each one to find out what it means.

subject: ela
text: This little prince was real. His name was Edward, and he lived in England about five hundred years ago. Stories say a friend of his took his punishments, but nobody knows if that’s true. In our book, it’s the rule, and Jemmy is the one who pays.

subject: ela
text: Hello again, it’s Opti. Today we open a brand-new book, The Whipping Boy. Here’s something to think about: what if you got in trouble every time someone else broke a rule? Hold on to that question. First you’ll warm up your words, then you’ll read the first two chapters, and at the end you’ll decide what you think of the prince.

subject: ela
text: Word work first. Today you’ll match some long words to what they mean, and you’ll go hunting for joining words inside sentences. A joining word never comes alone. It brings a whole chunk of the sentence along with it. See if you can catch the word and its chunk together.

subject: ela
text: Before you read: the castle is about to disappear behind you. Chapter 3 happens at night, and Chapter 4 happens in a thick fog. Watch Jemmy closely. He’s thinking hard the whole time, even when he’s quiet. And keep an eye out for a glowing light.

subject: ela
text: Yesterday you wrote a claim. Today you give it a reason, the because behind your opinion. A strong reason comes from something a character really did, not just how you feel. Look back at today’s chapters and pick the one moment that proves your point best.

subject: ela
text: Hi, it’s Opti. Last time you met a prince who never gets punished and a boy who always does. Today the prince has a big idea, and it isn’t a good one. As you read, ask yourself: is being bored a good enough reason to drag someone else into danger? Then you’ll give your opinion a reason to stand on.

subject: ela
text: Today the word work asks you to use what you’ve learned. You’ll build words from their parts, fill in sentences with this week’s vocabulary, and join short sentences with the right joining word. Before you type, read each sentence in your head. Your ears often know the answer before your eyes do.

subject: ela
text: Before you read Chapter 5, a tip: notice the moment Jemmy uses his elbow instead of his voice. Authors often show what a character is thinking through what they do. And when the lantern comes close to the saddle, slow down. One small thing changes everything.

subject: ela
text: Today your opinion gets proof. A text example is a moment from the book that shows your reason is true, and you always say which chapter it came from. Go back to a chapter, find the moment, and tell what happened in your own words.

subject: ela
text: Look closely at a king’s things, and you’ll often find his family’s signs, like lions and crowns. When the outlaws spot the king’s crest on the saddle, they know where that horse came from. Now it’s your turn. Design a crest that tells the world something about you.

subject: ela
text: Hello, it’s Opti. Our runaways are in real trouble now. Two rough men have found them in the fog, and one of the boys can’t seem to stop talking. Today, think about this: when you’re in danger, is it smarter to stay quiet or to speak up? Watch what each boy chooses.

subject: ela
text: Word study review day. You’ll roll some dice, fix joining words that don’t fit, and fill in sentences with words from all week. When something feels tricky, think back to Day 1. The patterns haven’t changed. You’ve just gotten better at spotting them.

subject: ela
text: No new chapters today. Instead, think back over the whole story so far. Picture the feast, the tower, the fog, and the outlaws. Which moment tells you the most about the prince? Which one tells you the most about Jemmy? Keep those two moments in mind.

subject: ela
text: Time to be your own editor. Read your claim, your reason, and your example out loud. Does each part do its job? Does your example really prove your reason? Find one thing to make stronger. Even great writers fix their work before anyone else reads it.

subject: ela
text: Welcome back, it’s Opti. Today we look back at all five chapters. One boy has fine clothes and a king for a father. The other has rags and a lot of whacks.
